edits.old: In standard Lambda, scale-out adds execution environments as simultaneous requests exceed available environments. Each environment can hold its own MongoClient and independent pool, so client reuse within warm environments does not make total Atlas connection demand independent of Lambda scale. OneUptime's serverless example illustrates this multiplication but does not report a measured Atlas capacity result. (high confidence)
edits.new: In standard Lambda, scale-out adds execution environments when no pre-initialized environment is available for a request. Each MongoClient instance manages its own connection pool, so if each execution environment holds its own client, client reuse within warm environments does not make total Atlas connection demand independent of Lambda scale. Across many concurrent requests or short-lived execution environments, per-environment pools multiply the total number of open connections and can trigger connection storms. Sources: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/lambda-concurrency.html ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/administration/connection-pool-overview.md ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/troubleshooting/connection-storms.md

edits.old: Lambda can purge idle connections, so a cached client does not guarantee that every pooled socket remains usable across warm invocations. AWS recommends keep-alive behavior, and MongoDB's Lambda guidance says tuning maxIdleTimeMS can reduce serverless timeout errors. (medium confidence)

evidence.quote: Lambda purges idle connections over time. Attempting to reuse an idle connection when invoking a function will result in a connection error.
To maintain your persistent connection, use the keep-alive directive associated with your runtime.
Tuning your `maxIdleTimeMS` can help reduce the occurrence of timeout errors from your serverless functions.
